newsitem.title: USA: Surging dlr/mark mixed blessing for ailing Germany.
newsitem.headline: Surging dlr/mark mixed blessing for ailing Germany.

text.p: Roughly one month after G7 finance officials converged on Berlin amid worries about the strength of the dollar, the greenback has settled into a comfortably tight, lower range against the yen.

But the greenback's persistent climb against the mark could soon become a fresh source of concern for Germany despite its help in fueling growth in exports. The weaker mark has meant rising German import prices and hurt odds for a cut in German interest rates.
And further weakness could create problems for Germany in its bid for Economic and Monetary Union, economists said this week.
"For economic and political reasons the weakness in the deutschemark is definitely a concern for Germany," said Richard Gilhooly, international bond strategist at Banque Paribas in New York.
Against the mark, however, the dollar has risen more than six pfennigs -- or almost four percent -- over the same time period.

On Thursday, despite a smaller-than-expected rise in German unemployment for February and a firm gain in January industrial orders, the dollar popped above the 1.72 mark threshold for the first time since April of 1994.

And even as the dollar surged to near three-year highs against the mark, Michael Rogowski, the head of Germany's machine and plant construction industry association VDMA, said that a dollar exchange rate of 1.80 to 2.00 marks would be more appropriate given relative purchasing power levels in the U.S. and Germany.

With economists calling for another robust U.S. employment report on Friday, and an increasing number of Fed watchers expecting a hike in U.S. interest rates later this month, the dollar's upside potential against the mark appears strong.

"The Bundesbank is aware of the likelihood of higher interest rates in the U.S. which could give the dollar some additional fire power ... and the last thing they want right now is a rapid weakening of the mark," said Chris Iggo, chief economist at BZW Securities Inc.

"There's a point where currency weakness starts to have negative implications for a country in terms of inflation and interest rates," he added. "Germany is probably not there yet, but at 1.80 (marks per dollar) it probably would be."
Iggo said his target for dollar/mark was 1.80, but conceded that a rise to 1.85 was not out of the question.
Reflecting concerns about further dollar appreciation against the mark, Bundesbank officials have grown more vocal about the German currency's weakness in recent weeks.

On Monday, Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke said the mark's depreciation should not continue and that the unit's rise to post-war highs against the dollar in early 1995 had now been fully corrected.

He said he saw no danger of an increase in Germany's inflationary trend at the current dollar/mark level -- which stood just below 1.70 on the day of his remarks -- but cautioned that import prices were rising.
Import prices jumped 2.6 percent in the year to January, and although weak German domestic demand should make it difficult for corporations to pass on price hikes, economists are wary.
In addition to inflation concerns, which are currently relatively minimal, they said that a weak mark poses other problems for Germany.
"I think the Bundesbank and German politicians, more generally, are very concerned about the declining deutschemark," said Paribas' Gilhooly.

"The Bundesbank (is concerned) because import prices are already picking up ... and the politicans because a collapsing deutschemark makes it difficult for them to sell the EMU concept to the public at large."

Compounding the mark's problems have been recent rumors of a delay in Europe's plan to launch a single currency by January 1999. While such talk has historically boosted the mark against the dollar, it has done little to help the German currency outside of Europe lately.
Economists said it appears that Germany's underlying economic weakness has begun to overshadow its status as a safe haven in times of EMU turbulence.

"Germany is in the thick of it now -- it's Germany's inability to meet the Maastricht criteria that's causing the delay rumors," said Marc Chandler, senior currency strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, explaining the mark's failure to benefit from EMU doubts.
Chandler was skeptical that current mark weakness was worrisome for Germany, but is predicting further dollar strength against the mark in the coming weeks.
"As long as these economic forces are intact the dollar can continue to go up," he said, noting that he expects the dollar to approach 1.75 marks by early April.
((-- N.A. Treasury Desk 212-859-1673))
